items.summary: Flow models have recently emerged as powerful generative priors for solving inverse problems. Despite their success, most existing flow-based inverse problem solvers initialize the reconstruction process with random Gaussian noise. However, recent studies in image generation have shown that the choice of initial noise can significantly influence generation outcomes. The role of initialization as a distinct design choice in flow-based inverse problem solving remains comparatively underexplored. In this work, we systematically evaluate noise initialization strategies while holding the downstream flow-based inverse solver fixed. We propose Retrieval-Augmented Initialization with Dual-Guided Inversion (RA-DGI), a method that constructs improved initial noise by leveraging retrieved proxy clean images and dual-guided inversion. Extensive experiments across multiple inverse problems demonstrate that the quality of the initial noise substantially affects reconstruction fidelity and perceptual performance. RA-DGI outperforms standard random initialization and achieves superior results compared to inference-time scaling strategies, while requiring less computational overhead. These findings highlight initialization as a critical yet previously overlooked factor in flow-based inverse problem solvers.
items.title: Retrieval-Augmented Initialization with Dual-Guided Inversion for Flow-Based Inverse Problem Solvers

items.summary: Reproduction material for the manuscript "Detection is not localization: a sampling-aware identifiability budget for change-point studies in electronic health records" (submitted to the Journal of Biomedical Informatics). Contents: 1. Simulation code for the two-phase Poisson panel with AR(1) frailty, implementing decision rules S0-S4 (analytic bound, oracle-boundary estimator, fixed-threshold search, wild-bootstrap-calibrated search, exact boundary recovery). 2. The two-stage design with the observable Delta BIC-gap stopping rule. 3. Component experiments: multiple-testing calibration, informative sampling with inverse-intensity weighting, conditional borrowing, relay measurement error. 4. Sampling-audit scripts for the PhysioNet/CinC Challenge 2012 (4,000 ICU stays) and 2019 sepsis (20,029 records) cohorts. 5. The full grid and all derived analysis tables reported in the manuscript and the supplementary material. All seeds are fixed; every reported cell is deterministic. items.summary: This paper is concerned with an inverse source problem for the stochastic fractional Helmholtz equation in a three-dimensional inhomogeneous medium. The source is modeled as real Gaussian spatial white noise with an unknown nonnegative strength function. For admissible frequencies, we establish well-posedness of the radiating solution in the distributional sense and show that it has a smooth representation outside the source region. For the inverse problem, by using two-point correlations of the field measured in an exterior open set at a single frequency, we prove a logarithmic stability estimate for recovering the source strength under an a priori Sobolev bound. As a uniform Hölder stability estimate is unavailable for the general admissible class, by assuming the difference between two source strengths has a fixed sign, we improve the stability to Hölder continuity with an optimal Hölder exponent. The analysis combines scattering theory and quantitative continuation for the fractional Laplacian using the Caffarelli-Silvestre extension.
items.title: Inverse source problem for the stochastic fractional Helmholtz equation in inhomogeneous media

items.summary: We study the local differential geometry of a Fourier-based modular-addition circuit in a one-layer transformer whose algorithm has previously been reverse-engineered. For each of the five key Fourier frequencies, we restrict the model's multilayer perceptron (MLP) contribution to a corresponding Fourier input plane and readout, and measure its directional Beltrami coefficient under continuous input perturbations. Whereas nondegenerate restrictions of ideal complex multiplication are conformal, the trained maps exhibit nonconformal distortion (median $|μ|=0.304$--$0.446$), spatial organization in the Beltrami argument, and regions of local orientation reversal. The median across frequencies decreases from $0.939$ at initialization to $0.390$ after training. The key-frequency planes also show lower median distortion than most random-plane controls, although their distributions overlap and the coordinate frames differ in conditioning. Across 500 checkpoints in one training run, most of the aggregate reduction in Beltrami magnitude occurs before the principal increase in the measured Fourier-circuit formation. At the individual-input level, Beltrami magnitude shows negligible association with the correct-logit margin ($|ρ|\leq0.026$). Late-checkpoint measurements across six runs show comparable distortion for most selected frequencies. These results provide a quantitative characterization of local deformation in a frequency-projected component of an identified neural circuit, complementary to its algorithmic reconstruction.
items.title: Nonconformal Distortion and Local Orientation Reversal in the Fourier Circuit of a Modular-Addition Transformer

items.summary: We study the critical Sobolev-curl quotient on $\mathbb{R}^3$ at the conformally invariant exponent $p=3/2$. Its sharp constant and optimizers were posed as open problems in the literature. We identify the toroidal and poloidal extremals. Two structural facts are used. First, the critical curl--curl equation is self-dual: the map $u\mapsto|\nabla\times u|^{-1/2}\nabla\times u$ is an involution on finite-energy solutions. It is the self-dual case of a duality between the exponents $p$ and $3p/(4p-3)$, which exchanges toroidal and poloidal fields and relates the sharp constants. Second, the toroidal minimization problem reduces exactly to a subcritical $3/2$-Laplace problem on the hyperbolic plane. Combined with symmetry and shooting results, these facts show that the two restricted sharp constants coincide. They also classify the gauge-minimal extremals: these are unique up to scaling and the Euclidean transformations realizing hyperbolic isometries, semi-explicit, and dual to each other. For nonzero one-signed profiles radial about a fixed hyperbolic centre, a gauge-canonical inverse of the duality yields an iteration by one-dimensional quadratures: the quotients are nonincreasing and converge to the restricted sharp constant, while the normalized iterates converge to the extremal pair. The first step from an explicit competitor gives the new upper bound $96\sqrt{15}π/(5\sqrt{4455π-13568})\approx11.2948$ for the restricted constants. The unrestricted sharp constant remains open. As an application, bounded axisymmetric poloidal potentials admit no $L^2$ zero mode of the Weyl-Dirac operator. An explicit conformal transformation extends this exclusion to both extremals at every real coupling.
items.title: Critical curl extremals and the hyperbolic plane

items.summary: Large gaps in seismic acquisition disrupt reflection events and hinder spectral recovery. Existing seismic interpolation deep unfolding networks primarily rely on localized spatial priors, limiting their ability to aggregate the global context necessary for reconstructing these extensive missing regions. We propose a spatial-spectral interactive projection-onto-convex-sets network (SSI-POCS) to tackle this severely ill-posed problem. By unfolding the classical iterative solver, our network integrates physical consistency with dual-domain deep priors via learned transforms, soft thresholding, and exact data reinsertion. Within the learned prior, a spatial Restormer branch captures local waveform structures, while a fast Fourier convolution (FFC) branch extracts global context, effectively suppressing incoherent components and enhancing spectral energy concentration in the $f-k$ domain. A dual-domain fusion module exchanges these complementary features via bidirectional channel attention and gated modulation, yielding substantial interpolation improvements. To overcome the severe loss of lateral continuity caused by large gaps, we introduce structural similarity (SSIM) supervision, complemented by focal frequency loss (FFL) and transform consistency constraints to suppress incoherent high-frequency components and regularize training. Experiments on a synthetic salt dome and a North Sea field dataset under 50% random and consecutive trace removal demonstrate the effectiveness of SSI-POCS. It significantly enhances event continuity across large gaps and mitigates artifacts, achieving a 3.285~dB SNR improvement over the best competing method while reducing parameters by 75.66%.
items.title: Spatial-Spectral Interactive POCS Network for Large-Gap Seismic Data Interpolation

items.summary: Flapping-wing simulation must reconcile high-frequency wingbeat aerodynamics with the slower dynamics relevant to flight control and reinforcement learning. We present FlapSim, a modular open-source MuJoCo simulation platform that combines robot descriptions, wing geometry, and composable aerodynamic models in a deterministic simulation pipeline. Across $48$ held-out scenarios spanning frequency, gimbal, wind, frequency-step, gust, and cross-robot flat-plate regimes, we compare five reduced-order configurations operating at $1\,\text{ms}$ with a $50\,μ\text{s}$ quasi-steady blade-element reference. The built-in hover cycle-averaged baseline achieves a $67.51\times$ CPU speedup but only $0.6593$ mean wrench fidelity. Combining multirate $21$-substep clock synchronization, three-dimensional linear/quadratic inflow and gust coupling, analytical blade-element geometry scaling, and phase-locked $1f\text{--}6f$ harmonics raises mean fidelity to $0.9646$ at a $65.19\times$ speedup in a five-block model. A streamlined four-block model without explicit step-transient lag states achieves $0.9662$ fidelity at a $67.98\times$ speedup. Controlled ablations show that stroke harmonics are particularly important during frequency transitions, improving held-out frequency-step fidelity by $+0.3176$. Transfer-function analysis explains this effect: fixed-window cycle averaging retains harmonic contributions when the wingbeat frequency changes, so within-cycle reconstruction also improves the filtered wrench. Once phase alignment and harmonic synthesis are included, explicit transient lag states provide no additional benefit in this benchmark. These results characterize the accuracy--computation tradeoff of the aerodynamic hierarchy and identify timing, inflow, geometry, and harmonic representation as central considerations for reduced-order flapping-wing simulation.
items.title: FlapSim: A Composable MuJoCo Simulation Platform and Reduced-Order Aerodynamic Model Hierarchy for Flapping-Wing Robotics

items.summary: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting has become a standard reasoning strategy in Multi-modal Large Language Models (MLLMs), showing strong performance in complex vision-language tasks such as reasoning segmentation. However, our analysis reveals that indiscriminate CoT usage can lead to degraded performance by inducing unnecessary reasoning, a phenomenon we term overthinking. In reasoning segmentation, overthinking often leads to misalignment between the query's intent and visual grounding. To address this, we propose Difficulty-Aware Chain-of-Thought (DA-CoT), a training-free adaptive framework that selectively triggers CoT based on the input's intrinsic difficulty. We find that the entropy of the model's attention maps reliably reflects task difficulty: low entropy indicates confident, localized grounding, while high entropy suggests uncertainty and potential benefit from CoT. DA-CoT uses this entropy signal to determine whether to apply CoT prompting. Additionally, we introduce a Bidirectional Rethinking mechanism that enables the model to automatically flip its reasoning decision when the initial output fails, enhancing robustness by recovering from failures induced by overthinking and underthinking. DA-CoT demonstrates its effectiveness by achieving state-of-the-art performance on the Reasoning Segmentation benchmarks while significantly improving inference efficiency.
items.title: Attention Maps Know When to Think: Training-Free Difficulty-Aware Chain-of-Thought for Reasoning Segmentation

items.summary: Phylogenetic networks provide a natural framework for representing reticulate evolutionary events such as horizontal gene transfer and hybridization. In the present manuscript, we investigate the identifiability of phylogenetic networks under (hardwired) parsimony, a natural extension of Maximum Parsimony from trees to networks. More precisely, we ask which structural features of a network can be uniquely inferred from so-called $A_k$-alignments under this criterion. While identifiability has been studied extensively for phylogenetic trees under parsimony, little is known about the identifiability of networks under hardwired parsimony. We take a first step towards addressing this gap by developing a general framework for studying identifiability under hardwired parsimony. We then use this framework to show that the tree of blobs of a phylogenetic network can be reconstructed from its $A_1$-alignment. This result can be viewed as a natural extension of Buneman's well-known splits equivalence theorem. Finally, we show that, under hardwired parsimony, cycles of length at least $5$ cannot in general be uniquely identified from character data, establishing a fundamental limitation of hardwired parsimony.
items.title: An extension of the classic Buneman theorem from phylogenetic trees to networks

items.summary: Although self-improvement is becoming increasingly important as tasks become more complex, models struggle to generate reliable supervision for harder, out-of-distribution instances. One way to address this challenge is to exploit compositional structure: models often solve simpler subproblems more reliably than full problems, so their subproblem predictions can be composed into supervision for harder ones. We systematically study when this kind of composed supervision supports self-improvement and when it fails. Our controlled experiments identify three failure modes: unreliable subproblem predictions, errors introduced by composition, and limited supervision coverage. Beyond controlled settings, these findings carry over to more realistic coding and reasoning tasks: composed labels are more accurate than direct self-generated labels and improve performance even on compositions longer than those seen during training, while the failure modes remain visible. items.summary: Distributionally robust optimization (DRO) minimizes worst-case risk under distributional uncertainty, but its decisions can be suboptimal in terms of their excess risk, or regret. Here, a wide spectrum of simple algorithms, including DRO, achieve the instance-optimal rate of $O(κ\varepsilon^2)$. For fixed $\varepsilon > 0$, we prove that DRO still achieves the minimax rate if the problem has bounded residual effective rank. On the other hand, we identify significant failure modes where DRO is provably suboptimal by dimension-dependent factors. Fortunately, we prove that two alternative procedures, minimax regret optimization (MRO) and spectral-norm regularization (SNR), attain the minimax rate. We derive an exact convex reformulation of MRO and an accelerated proximal algorithm for SNR, along with high-probability finite-sample guarantees. We support these theoretical results with numerical experiments separating the performance of MRO and SNR from DRO.

items.summary: Spatial reasoning in Vision-Language Models (VLMs) has increasingly benefited from tool-integrated pipelines that ground computation in explicit geometry. However, existing systems often compile queries into relatively open-ended artifacts, such as code, task constraints, tool plans, or gathered evidence, leaving what must be resolved before execution under-specified. This can lead to unnecessary tool acquisition and iterative refinement, while still producing plausible reasoning traces from incomplete spatial commitments. We identify this failure mode as under-committed query compilation. To address it, we propose PEPS, a training-free agentic paradigm Parsing Executable Primitives for Spatial reasoning under a typed FESM schema over Frame, Entity, State, and Metric. PEPS follows a parse-before-execute principle: the Parser commits each query to a compact set of executable requirements; the Executor selectively grounds the required primitives through fixed geometric APIs and deterministic computation; and the Verifier checks execution sufficiency, enabling early termination or targeted repair. Extensive experiments across challenging spatial reasoning benchmarks show that PEPS consistently improves reasoning accuracy while substantially reducing refinement rounds, API cost, and end-to-end latency over strong tool-integrated baselines. These results demonstrate that explicit requirement commitment can make tool-integrated spatial reasoning not only more reliable, but also more execution-efficient.

items.summary: Support points provide a practical and effective way to approximate a probability distribution by a small set of equally weighted representatives through energy-distance minimization. In many applications, the variables satisfy convex constraints that the representatives should also respect. We investigate whether unconstrained support points automatically satisfy such constraints and show that this is not guaranteed. We construct counterexamples using three planar observations, a density with full triangular support, and positive-definite matrix data admitting an indefinite optimal representative under the Frobenius norm. We also identify cases in which containment holds, establish stability under distributional perturbations, and quantify the objective cost of imposing a convex-hull constraint. For a fixed number of representatives and a positive population constraint gap, empirical configurations with vanishing global objective error eventually leave the sample convex hull almost surely.

Symmetric Holdout Evaluation (n = 2,000; seed 42): Calibrated Time-to-Collision (TTC) and Random Forest both achieve F2 = 0.9103; XGBoost achieves F2 = 0.9065. items.summary: Flapping-wing simulation must reconcile high-frequency wingbeat aerodynamics with the slower dynamics relevant to flight control and reinforcement learning. We present FlapSim, a modular open-source MuJoCo simulation platform that combines robot descriptions, wing geometry, and composable aerodynamic models in a deterministic simulation pipeline. Across $48$ held-out scenarios spanning frequency, gimbal, wind, frequency-step, gust, and cross-robot flat-plate regimes, we compare five reduced-order configurations operating at $1\,\text{ms}$ with a $50\,μ\text{s}$ quasi-steady blade-element reference. The built-in hover cycle-averaged baseline achieves a $67.51\times$ CPU speedup but only $0.6593$ mean wrench fidelity. Combining multirate $21$-substep clock synchronization, three-dimensional linear/quadratic inflow and gust coupling, analytical blade-element geometry scaling, and phase-locked $1f\text{--}6f$ harmonics raises mean fidelity to $0.9646$ at a $65.19\times$ speedup in a five-block model. A streamlined four-block model without explicit step-transient lag states achieves $0.9662$ fidelity at a $67.98\times$ speedup. Controlled ablations show that stroke harmonics are particularly important during frequency transitions, improving held-out frequency-step fidelity by $+0.3176$. Transfer-function analysis explains this effect: fixed-window cycle averaging retains harmonic contributions when the wingbeat frequency changes, so within-cycle reconstruction also improves the filtered wrench. Once phase alignment and harmonic synthesis are included, explicit transient lag states provide no additional benefit in this benchmark. These results characterize the accuracy--computation tradeoff of the aerodynamic hierarchy and identify timing, inflow, geometry, and harmonic representation as central considerations for reduced-order flapping-wing simulation.
items.title: FlapSim: A Composable MuJoCo Simulation Platform and Reduced-Order Aerodynamic Model Hierarchy for Flapping-Wing Robotics

items.summary: Dexterous robotic manipulation remains a major challenge in robotics, exemplified by piano playing, which requires coordinated control of fingers and provides a demanding testbed for reinforcement learning (RL). Although previous work established a benchmark for robotic piano playing, it is restricted to two hands and does not support unified evaluation. To address this gap, we introduce OmniPiano, a benchmark that provides one to up to five Shadow Hands and supports standard, robust, safe, and multi-agent RL within a shared piano-playing task family. OmniPiano is developed for scalable and diverse piano-playing tasks with configurable perturbations, explicit safety constraints, and decentralized cooperation settings. Particularly, to facilitate usability and extendability, OmniPiano adopts a highly modular design and provides comprehensive tasks to support RL study of task performance, robustness, safety, and cooperation in dexterous control. With at least 912 task settings and 36 baseline algorithms, OmniPiano further incorporates LLM-based agents to broaden the evaluation scope and reveal new insights. Extensive evaluations show that state-of-the-art RL algorithms and frontier LLM-based agents still struggle on challenging piano-playing tasks, even under standard RL settings, highlighting substantial room for improvement in dexterous control. The code, dataset, tutorial, and demo are available at https://sail-research-lab.github.io/omnipiano/.
items.title: OmniPiano: Diverse Dexterous Piano-Playing Challenges for Standard, Robust, Safe, and Multi-Agent RL

items.summary: Machine learning can screen far more candidates than can be experimentally validated, creating a need for selection procedures that identify promising candidates while controlling risk before costly experimental validation. We propose Uncertainty-Normalized Empirical Calibration (UNEC), a p-value-free framework that ranks candidates by uncertainty-normalized predictive margins and directly calibrates a selection cutoff using held-out losses. UNEC supports flexible prediction models, general bounded losses, and diverse selection targets. We study marginal discovery risk (MDR) and selective discovery risk (SDR), with SDR reducing to the false discovery rate under binary loss. We establish finite-sample MDR control for an adjusted rule and asymptotic SDR control with explicit limiting risk and power. Under a location--scale model with a common one-sided binary target, we further show that UNEC asymptotically attains the oracle power benchmark among observation-wise selection rules. Simulations and molecular screening applications in solubility, toxicity, and lipophilicity demonstrate favorable risk--power trade-offs and substantial computational gains across binary and graded-loss settings.
items.title: Power-Optimal Risk Control via Standardized Margin Calibration

items.summary: LLM-as-a-judge systems often aggregate multiple judges to improve evaluation reliability. However, judge agreement can reflect shared biases toward verbosity, formatting, or fluency rather than the intended evaluation target. Addressing these shared biases is challenging because observational judge outputs alone cannot distinguish agreement driven by target quality from agreement driven by nuisance attributes. We introduce VoirDire, an intervention-calibrated aggregation method for LLM-judge panels. VoirDire applies controlled interventions that vary specified surface attributes while aiming to preserve the evaluation target; it then uses paired changes in judge scores to identify nuisance-sensitive directions. It attenuates these directions and selects aggregation weights that retain variation across items while penalizing sensitivity to the interventions, making the final consensus less dependent on superficial features. We show theoretically that observational judge outputs alone cannot identify which shared direction is target-relevant, while paired interventions provide the contrast needed to identify nuisance-sensitive variation. We evaluate VoirDire on 12 datasets spanning continuous scoring, binary classification, and pairwise preference. Compared with the existing LLM-judge aggregation baselines, VoirDire reduces MAE by up to 26.8% on continuous-score tasks and improves accuracy by up to 5.3 percentage points on binary and preference tasks. These findings suggest that counterfactual interventions provide an additional means of improving the reliability and controllability of LLM-based evaluation beyond merely relying on observed judge agreement.
items.title: VoirDire: Counterfactual Calibration for Reliable LLM-as-a-Judge Aggregation

items.summary: Multi-turn negotiation remains a challenging problem for large language model (LLM) agents. While LLMs can conduct natural-language dialogue, existing benchmarks predominantly assess only agreement rates, overlooking whether negotiated commitments actually create value once executed. To address this gap, we introduce TradeWar, a multi-country simulation benchmark that translates negotiation dialogues into concrete tariff and trade-share policies, enforces capacity and network constraints during settlement, and evaluates outcomes via an Economic Health Index (EHI). To solve this execution-grounded task, we propose TACTIC (Trade-aware Adaptive Consolidation and Theory-of-mind for International Commerce), an agent that iteratively refines its negotiation strategy across episodes-without updating base LLM weights-by leveraging prior experience, opponent behavior, and past settlement outcomes. Despite using zero-shot chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting, PromptLLM attains a 75% agreement rate but only 57.1 final EHI (*100), whereas TACTIC reaches 68.8. Across 20 sequential episodes and three seeds, TACTIC's final EHI improves from 58.2 to 73.2, compared with 65.2 for an ablation without cross-episode updates. Under technology-controls and energy-crisis shocks, TACTIC also exhibits smaller performance degradation than PromptLLM and MemoryLLM. These results indicate that CoT deliberation and interaction memory alone do not fully address delayed execution feedback, whereas settlement-grounded adaptation improves long-horizon negotiation in TradeWar.
items.title: TradeWar: A Benchmark for Execution-Grounded Trade Negotiation with Adaptive LLM Agents

items.summary: Existing Graphical User Interface (GUI) benchmarks predominantly rely on precise and stateless user instructions. In everyday usage, however, instructions are often \emph{vague and history-dependent}: users omit the exact details of their past operations because they no longer remember them, leaving the agent to recover the missing context from long and noisy interaction histories. To bridge this evaluation gap, we introduce \textbf{MemU-Bench}, a mobile benchmark of \textbf{118 vague tasks} grounded in 29 long-horizon user trajectories, where agents must distill raw interaction streams into memory and retrieve the missing context on demand, with task outcomes verified against serialized application databases. Alongside Success Rate, we incorporate Interaction Efficiency (IE) and Success weighted by Path Length (SPL) to expose agents that succeed by exhaustively searching across different applications rather than by \emph{genuinely recalling} the history. Evaluations show that without user history, state-of-the-art systems struggle under such ambiguity: the best-performing Gemini-3.1-Pro achieves an SPL of only 16.4\%, and end-to-end GUI agents fall below 5\%. To address this, we further propose \textbf{AppMem}, a training-free framework that distills user history into a \emph{structured, app-centric} memory bank, tracks interrupted intents across application switches, and selectively retrieves relevant memories via target-app inference. AppMem raises the SPL of GPT-5.5 from 15.7\% to 66.9\% (\textbf{+51.2\%}), outperforms a naive summary baseline by 9.3\%, and delivers consistent gains across evaluated backbones.
items.title: MemU-Bench: Benchmarking GUI Agents on Long-Horizon User Interactions

items.summary: Coding agents working in shared repositories may receive separate, independently-motivated requests from human developers, creating a setting that is multi-agent by necessity. When this scenario happens, their individual implementations may work separately but conflict when combined. To study this setting, we introduce ParallACT, a benchmark of orchestrator-free multi-agent coding tasks. ParallACT contains both complementary and contradictory tasks. In complementary tasks, each agent's task is separately useful and implementations must share an interface to be productively combined. In contradictory pairs, both agents' tasks require editing the same code in incompatible ways, and naively combining independent solutions fails to produce a useful implementation. We compare a single-agent oracle given the combined set of tasks against multi-agent settings that vary execution order, visibility, awareness of other agents, and access to a communication channel. We find that the oracle solves most tasks while parallel agents perform substantially worse. Their performance drop is notable for complementary tasks, and particularly sharp for contradictory tasks (e.g., from 62% to 16% for Claude Code with Claude Opus 4.8) where merged code typically satisfies only one specification, and the same gap appears in all six further configurations pairing two agent harnesses with three open-weight models. Simply telling an agent that a peer exists does not help significantly, and giving agents access to a communication channel recovers only a small part of the performance, at an additional token cost. ParallACT thus identifies and isolates a core challenge that will become more common as multi-agent coding by independent principals becomes standard, and provides a controlled test of which coordination strategies help, and at what cost.
items.title: Decentralized Multi-Agent Coordination and Communication in Shared Codebases

items.summary: Natural-language driven smart home control remains challenging: cloud-hosted Large Language Models (LLMs) raise privacy concerns, while local Small Language Models (SLMs) can generate invalid actions or misinterpret requests. We introduce Trail (Typed Registry-Anchored Inference for Language commands in Smart Homes), a fully local framework that replaces open-ended command generation with hierarchical typed decisions. Trail exploits the natural structure of a home's action space, selecting a room, device, and operation from candidates derived from the runtime device registry. This ensures valid actions while enabling confidence-based abstention when requests cannot be reliably resolved. We also design a structured memory module that uses typed decisions to support user preferences, device references, and multi-turn interactions. To evaluate Trail, we extend HomeBench and generate three datasets: Trek-Base, which tests natural-language variation; Trek-Robust, which evaluates robustness to changes in the home and its description; and Trek-Memory, which assesses conversational memory across multi-turn interactions. Trail achieves 85.3% accuracy on Trek-Robust versus 69.8% for a finetuned Qwen3.5-4B baseline, while remaining competitive on Trek-Base requests. With memory, Trail resolves 75.6% of the requests that depend on earlier turns, compared with 42.5% for the finetuned baseline given conversation history.
items.title: Trail: Accurate Local Smart Home Control Using Decision Models

items.summary: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting has become a standard reasoning strategy in Multi-modal Large Language Models (MLLMs), showing strong performance in complex vision-language tasks such as reasoning segmentation. However, our analysis reveals that indiscriminate CoT usage can lead to degraded performance by inducing unnecessary reasoning, a phenomenon we term overthinking. In reasoning segmentation, overthinking often leads to misalignment between the query's intent and visual grounding. To address this, we propose Difficulty-Aware Chain-of-Thought (DA-CoT), a training-free adaptive framework that selectively triggers CoT based on the input's intrinsic difficulty. We find that the entropy of the model's attention maps reliably reflects task difficulty: low entropy indicates confident, localized grounding, while high entropy suggests uncertainty and potential benefit from CoT. DA-CoT uses this entropy signal to determine whether to apply CoT prompting. Additionally, we introduce a Bidirectional Rethinking mechanism that enables the model to automatically flip its reasoning decision when the initial output fails, enhancing robustness by recovering from failures induced by overthinking and underthinking. DA-CoT demonstrates its effectiveness by achieving state-of-the-art performance on the Reasoning Segmentation benchmarks while significantly improving inference efficiency.
items.title: Attention Maps Know When to Think: Training-Free Difficulty-Aware Chain-of-Thought for Reasoning Segmentation
